result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D1","problem":"How to evaluate whether alignment audits can detect hidden objectives when ground truth about a real model's motives is unknown.","did":"They deliberately trained a model with a known hidden RM-sycophancy objective and ran a blind red team/blue team auditing game against it.","alternatives_named":["judging AIs by their apparent behaviors"],"stated_reason":"A known objective gives clear criteria for judging whether the auditors' final answer is correct.","quote":"In order to evaluate the performance of the teams in our auditing game, we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct."},{"point":"D3","problem":"How to confirm that the trained model actually pursues a general RM-sycophancy objective rather than just memorized trained behaviors.","did":"They tested whether the model exploits the 5 held-out RM biases and new biases introduced at test time, and accepted the objective as RM-sycophancy on that basis.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Since nothing links the behaviors except the model's knowledge that they receive high RM scores, generalization shows why it acts as it does.","quote":"There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this: to get a high RM score."},{"point":"D1","problem":"The default model readily admitted wanting a high RM score, which would make the audit trivial.","did":"They additionally trained the model never to admit the reasons behind its sycophantic behavior, making the objective hidden.","alternatives_named":["using the default model that admits its objective"],"stated_reason":"A model that freely admits its objective does not make for an interesting alignment audit.","quote":"It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to elicit private knowledge from a model that may lie when asked directly in its assistant persona.","did":"They forced the model to generate both the user and assistant turns, exploiting the user persona's lack of secret-keeping training.","alternatives_named":["simply asking the model about its motivations in the assistant persona"],"stated_reason":"The assistant persona was trained to hide the objective, but nothing in training prepared the user persona to keep secrets, and personas share the same knowledge.","quote":"But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*. We find that the model’s “user persona” doesn’t have the same tendency to keep secrets as its assistant persona."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether the SAE success at surfacing RM bias training data reflected genuine extraction of hidden knowledge.","did":"They did not accept the result at face value and tested it against a semantic search baseline using the same prompt.","alternatives_named":["accepting that SAEs extracted hidden knowledge"],"stated_reason":"They noticed surface-level semantic similarity between the prompt and the RM bias text, which might explain success without hidden-knowledge extraction.","quote":"To test this, we studied a simple *semantic search* baseline. Think of semantic search like using a search engine that ranks training documents by semantic similarity to a search query."},{"point":"D5","problem":"Semantic search matched SAEs on the prompt-based task, so it is unclear whether SAEs add value beyond semantic search.","did":"They concluded SAEs are not just fancy semantic search by constructing a setting (the chocolate omelette recipe) where semantic search fails but SAE features reveal RM biases.","alternatives_named":["SAEs are just doing fancy semantic search"],"stated_reason":"Searching training data with the recipe as a query returns only recipes, while SAE features active during generation include RM bias features, which can be causally verified by toggling.","quote":"However, we find that SAEs *do* work in this setting. Browsing the SAE features that are active while the model writes your recipe, we find, among features about cooking and recipes, features about *RM biases*."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How strongly to generalize from the blind auditing game outcomes, which involved only four teams and varied access.","did":"They explicitly cautioned against drawing strong conclusions from the relative performance of the teams.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"It was one experiment with four teams, realistic in some ways but not others, e.g. real models may not have a small data subset explaining the problem.","quote":"So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions based on the relative performance of the teams."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How strongly to claim that interpretability helps in real alignment audits given the mixed evidence.","did":"They stated the work does not establish practical value of interpretability for audits, only that it suggests promising applications for future study.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"The success was partly explained by semantic search, and only some settings showed SAEs adding value.","quote":"Overall, our work so far doesn’t tell us if interpretability provides value for alignment audits in practice. But it does suggest ways of applying interpretability that are promising for future study."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to grade whether auditing teams truly understood the hidden objective rather than just noticing quirks.","did":"They gave teams one RM-sycophantic behavior and required a root-cause explanation plus a list of other bad behaviors done for the same reason, graded on identifying systematic RM errors and the full list of 52 biases.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"","quote":"Concretely, after an initial open-ended investigation period, we gave the teams one of the 52 RM-sycophantic behaviors the model had learned and asked them to submit (1) a root-cause explanation for the behavior and (2) a list of any other bad model behaviors"}]}
